title: The Sleeping Pill Your Doctor Prescribed May Be Wrecking Your Morning Drive. A World-First Trial Just Proved It.
excerpt: Low-dose quetiapine — increasingly prescribed off-label for insomnia — impaired next-day driving and slowed reaction times. One in four people did not even notice.
body:
A world-first clinical trial has found that a commonly prescribed sleeping pill leaves people too impaired to drive safely the next morning — and one in four of them do not even realise it.

The study, published in the Annals of the American Thoracic Society, examined low-dose quetiapine — sold as Seroquel — which is increasingly prescribed off-label for insomnia despite being approved only for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Researchers at Flinders University in Australia found that while the drug did help people sleep longer and wake less during the night, it significantly slowed reaction times and worsened driving performance in a simulator the following morning.

"There's a growing belief that low-dose quetiapine is a relatively harmless way to help people sleep," said lead author Cricket Fauska, a PhD candidate at the Flinders Health and Medical Research Institute. "Our results show it's not that simple."

The Hidden Impairment

Fifteen participants with obstructive sleep apnoea and co-existing insomnia — a combination that affects an estimated 30 to 40 per cent of sleep apnoea patients — were given either 25 milligrams of quetiapine or a placebo before bed. The next morning, they completed a battery of cognitive tests and a driving simulator session.

The results were sobering. Participants on quetiapine drifted out of their lane more frequently and showed measurably slower reaction times. Eleven of the fifteen reported feeling sleepier. But roughly one in four did not recognise their level of impairment — meaning they might have driven to work, dropped children at school, or operated machinery without knowing their reflexes were compromised.

The researchers now recommend avoiding driving or any safety-critical task for at least 9.5 hours after taking quetiapine.

Why This Matters for the South Asian Diaspora

Quetiapine prescriptions have exploded in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia over the past decade. In the US alone, off-label prescriptions for insomnia now account for an estimated 45 to 55 per cent of all quetiapine use, according to pharmacy dispensing data. The drug is cheap, widely available as a generic, and sits in a regulatory grey zone: physicians can prescribe it for sleep even though it was never tested or approved for that purpose.

South Asian Americans and British Indians face a particular convergence of risk factors. Long work hours, high-stress careers in technology and medicine, and cultural reluctance to seek mental health treatment mean that when sleep problems become unbearable, the first intervention is often a pill rather than a behavioural programme. Quetiapine, with its reputation as "not a real sleeping pill," has become a quiet favourite among primary care physicians treating South Asian patients who resist being prescribed traditional sedatives.

The Flinders study suggests that quiet favourite may be quietly dangerous.

What Women Should Know

Dr Ashley Curtis, director of the Cognition, Aging, Sleep and Health Lab at the University of South Florida, flagged an additional concern: women generally metabolise sedative medications more slowly than men, which can amplify both the therapeutic effect and the next-morning hangover.

"Future studies should carefully examine whether these newer agents demonstrate similar sex-specific patterns to ensure optimal dosing and safety recommendations," she said.

The FDA issued a similar warning about zolpidem — the active ingredient in Ambien — in 2013, halving the recommended dose for women after studies showed dangerous levels of the drug in the bloodstream the morning after. No equivalent adjustment has been made for quetiapine, largely because its use as a sleep aid was never formally studied at scale until now.

The Bigger Picture

The study is small — fifteen participants, one night each — and the researchers are cautious about drawing sweeping conclusions. But it is the first randomised trial to measure quetiapine's impact on next-day driving performance, and the findings align with a growing body of evidence that off-label sedative use carries risks that neither patients nor prescribers fully appreciate.

For the millions of South Asians in the diaspora who struggle with sleep — whether from jet lag on India trips, shift work, or the chronic stress of immigration — the message is not to stop seeking help for insomnia. It is to ask sharper questions about what you are being prescribed and why.

Sources: Annals of the American Thoracic Society (June 2026); Flinders University press release; University of South Florida commentary; FDA zolpidem safety communication (2013)
